Phonotactic constraints define what sound sequences are possible and what other
sound sequences are not possible in a given language. These constrains are based on
an examination of what sequences occur and what sequences do not occur in that
language. This scheme works as far as patterns either really never occur or, if they do,
they are very common. The problem is that some patterns occur, but are very rare, and
it is not immediately clear whether we should take them to be allowed or disallowed by
our phonotactic constraints. As an example, think of ʃw in English: this sound sequence
occurs in compound words (like dishwasher dɪ́ʃwɔʃə), some names
(like Gershwin gə́ːʃwɪn, Schwartzenegger ʃwóːtsənɛgə, or Schweppes ʃwɛ́ps) and a
single one-morpheme common noun, schwa ʃwɑ́ː, which is a linguistic technical term.
This is significant because neither morphologically complex words, nor names are very
relevant in identifying phonotactic constraints, so there remains a single “real”
representative of this cluster, the realness of which is jeopardized by its being unknown
to very many speakers of English.

If we construe phonotactic constraints that allow ʃw, we will be faced with the question
why there are so few instances of this cluster in English. The common practice is to not
allow ʃw, and list it as an exception. The reason for doing so is our desire to formulate
phonotactic constraints in terms of natural classes: we will see that these constraints
involve not random sets of sounds, but groups that belong together because of their
inherent properties (like place or manner of articulation or voicing).

Because phonotactic constraints are formulated in broad terms, they cannot predict
exactly what sound strings are and what sound strings are not available in a language.

   MORPHOLOGY AND SYTANX
         (ENG509)

         Prepared By: Sajid Iqbal & Saira Hafeez

VIRTUAL UNIVERSITY OF PAKISTAN

                                                   1

                  ENG509 Lesson (20~36) Extracted from slides

➢ If an animal is innately programmed for some type of behaviour, then there are likely to be
  biological clues. (Mean something innate that is responsible for some particular behaviour, in
  linguistics we are searching for some innate thing which is responsible for language speaking)

➢ Fish have bodies which are streamlined and smooth, with fins and a powerful tail structurally
  adapted for moving fast through the water. (Body structure and physical behaviour of fish have
  resemblance)

➢ Biological clues are not essential. It is impossible to guess their behaviour from their bodies solely.
  (But these biological clues have some relevance)

➢ Birds make nests, and, sometimes, animals behave in a way quite contrary to what might be
  expected from their physical form.

➢ Changes in the form of the body or structural changes are the most direct indications of innate
  programming.

➢ Physiological adaptations include changes in the bodily functions, such as rate of heartbeat and
  breathing.

➢ If we look at the organs used in speech, humans seem to be somewhere in the middle between the
  obvious structural adaptation of birds to flying, and the apparent lack of correlation between birds
  and nest building.

➢ The human brain and vocal tract have a number of slightly unusual features which can not indicate
  sufficiently that people can talk. (Can be assumed by some analysis)

➢ If we assume that all humans speak a language, then biological facts can be viewed as partial
  adaptations of the body to the production of language.

➢ Another important difference between humans and monkeys concerns the larynx, which contains the
  ‘voice box’ or ‘vocal cords simpler in structure than that of other primates.

➢ This is an advantage as air can move freely past and then out through the nose and mouth
  without being hindered by other appendages. (As we have studied that human children and
  chimpanzees have same larynx so that they can drink and breathe together i.e. an infant sucking her
  mother)

➢ Human brain is very different in appearance from that of other animals.

                                                                                                       2

                  ENG509 Lesson (20~36) Extracted from slides

➢ Human brain is heavier than animals

➢ Human brain with more surface folding of the cortex, outer layer of ‘grey matter’ which surrounds
  the inner core of nerve fibres.

➢ In human brain, though grey matter is actually pink in live humans, it goes grey after death.

➢ Superficially, the brains of a chimp and a human have certain similarities.

➢ Language emerges at about the same time in children all over the world.

➢ Children normally begin to speak between their eighteenth and twenty-eighth months.

➢ It is suggested that language may be set in motion by a biological clock, similar to the one which
  causes kittens to open their eyes when they are a few days old.

➢ Behaviour that is triggered off biologically has a number of special characteristics.

➢ If it can be shown that speech, like sexual activities and the ability to walk, falls into the category of
  biologically scheduled behaviour.

➢ The behaviour emerges before it is necessary

➢ Appearance of behaviour is not the result of a conscious decision.

➢ Emergence of behaviour is not triggered by external events (though the surrounding environment
  must be sufficiently ‘rich’ for it to develop adequately).

➢ There is a regular sequence of ‘milestones’ as the behaviour develops, and these can usually be
  correlated with age and other aspects of development.

➢ There may be a ‘critical period’ for the acquisition of the behaviour.

➢ Direct teaching and intensive practice have relatively little effect.

➢ Although children differ enormously in their ability to knit or play the violin, their language
  proficiency varies to a much lesser extent.

➢ Children acquire language without making any conscious decision about it.

                                                                                                          3

                  ENG509 Lesson (20~36) Extracted from slides

➢ Children begin to talk even when their surroundings remain unchanged.

➢ Most of them live in the same house, eat the same food, have the same parents, and follow the same
  routine. No specific event or feature in their surroundings suddenly starts them off talking.

➢ Children do not manufacture any new brain cells after birth.

➢ They are born with millions, perhaps billions. At first the cells are not all interconnected, and the
  brain is relatively light (about 300g).

➢ From birth to around 2 years, many more cells interconnect, and brain weight increases rapidly. By
  the age of 2, it weighs nearly 1000g (Lenneberg1967).

➢ Although no external event causes the behaviour, the surrounding environment must be
  sufficiently ‘rich ‘for it to develop adequately.

➢ ‘Direct teaching and intensive practice have relatively little effect.’

➢ In activities such as typing or playing tennis, a person’s achievement is often directly related to the
  amount of teaching they receive and the hours of practice they put in. Not ‘naturally’ superb athletes
  can win.

➢ We may conclude, then, that mere practice – in the sense of direct repetition and imitation – does not
  affect the acquisition of language in a significant way

Question:
What do you think are the challenges or the limitations of morphology and syntax effectively? Discuss.
Answer:
Teaching morphology and syntax effectively challenging due to their complexity and theoretical nature. These are challenges and limitations that occurs in morphology and syntax:
Complexity:
 Morphology and syntax cause the complexity for the learners and make phonological and syntactic confusion in children so because of the similarities in structure students fail to retrieve and store new words.
Abstract concepts:
Understanding abstract like grammatical categories, syntactic rules and morphological processes can be difficult to learn without practical examples and hands-on activities.
Lack of universal grammar:
Every language is different from another but there are certain words that are common in many languages so when we learn a language it is very challenging to remember the same meaning.
Variation and flexibility:
Natural languages have variations and flexibilities in how morphological and syntactic rules are applied, making it challenging to present a unified set of rules.
Engagement and interest:
In morphology and syntax it is very challenging for learners keeping engaged, especially in dealing with linguistic concepts that may not seem immediately applicable or interesting.
Teacher expertise:
Teaching of morphology and syntax requires knowledgeable instructor who can explain these abstract concepts widely and provide very clear comprehension.
If we overcome these challenges we can bring many desirable changes in linguistics knowledge especial in language learning.

﻿ENG509
GDB
Yes, I agree with Chomsky’s idea of Universal Grammar to a large extent. Children are born with a natural ability to learn any language. This ability already exists in their brain, but language develops through exposure. Children learn language by observing the people around them, their environment, and daily interactions. By listening and watching, they learn a wide range of languages and gradually start forming sentences on their own. This shows that they already have an internal system that helps them learn language, which is then shaped by their surroundings.

Children learn language very differently from adults. Adults usually learn a language by first studying grammar rules. For example, when learning a language like Arabic, adults often begin with grammar, which can be difficult, and then move toward learning words and sentences. In contrast, children do not follow this process. They may speak incoherently at first or use incorrect and complex words, but they do not consciously construct grammar rules. They are not simply copying others; instead, they actively organize language in their own minds.

Chomsky’s theory of Universal Grammar explains this process by suggesting that basic grammatical rules are already present in the human mind at birth. However, the environment plays a crucial role. Regular exposure and social interaction are necessary for proper language development. Without exposure to language, full language development becomes difficult, regardless of natural ability. In my opinion, children are born with strong language potential, but environment, culture, and interaction shape that potential.

Q. Types of Determiners top
Articles: There are three articles in English language: a, an, the. The articles "a” and” an’ are used when we need
to clarify the noun as indefinite and singular. The article " a" comes before nouns beginning with a constant
sound, while the article "an" comes before nouns beginning with a vowel sound. The article "the" is used
when we need to clarify the noun as definite and unique.
Example of Articles: We saw the car again today.
Demonstratives: The category of words which is used to clarify the distance of something or some person
from the speaker is called demonstratives.
Use of Demonstratives in a Sentence: Demonstratives can function as adjectives and pronouns in a
sentence. These include: That, These, This, Those "That" is used when a singular noun is not very close to
the speaker. 'This" is used when a singular noun is precisely in front and close to the speaker. 'T hose" is
used when plural nouns are not very close to the speaker "These" is used when plural nouns are precisely
in front and close to the speaker.
Examples of Demonstratives: These books are fun to read.
Possessives: The words that come to modify a noun to indicate possession towards some person or
something are called possessives. These include: your, our, my, his, hers, its, their etc.
Examples of Possessives: I am doing my assignment.
Quantifiers: The category of indefinite determiners which is used to indicate the quantity of the noun
without stating the precise number is called the Quantifiers. These include: many, much, plenty, enough,
several, some, few, little etc.

Name any three 'head movement' in syntax?
In syntax, "head movement" refers to the process of moving a word or phrase to a position where
it can serve as the head of a phrase. Here are three examples of head movement:

1. Verb movement: In some languages, verbs move to a higher position in the sentence to mark
tense or agreement.

2. Auxiliary inversion: In English, auxiliary verbs like "will" or "can" move to the beginning of
a sentence to form a question.

3. Wh-movement: In questions, wh-words like "who", "what", or "where" move to the
beginning of the sentence to mark the question.

Wh-questions?
Questions which ask for a particular piece of information, rather than for simply Yes or No, are
called wh-questions. We call them wh -questions because they are often introduced by a word (or
phrase) beginning with wh-.

wh-questions

(I) Where did John hide the money?

(2) What did she say?

(3) When did he come back?

(4) Which girl did Bill like best?

(5) Who(m) did you meet there?

    ❖ However, the wh-word does not always open the question.
    ❖ It may also appear inside the first constituent of the sentence:

Inside wh-question
(6) For what reason did you leave early?

(7) In what way did John offend her?

(8) At what distance were you from that spot?

what is Superfluous information?
Superfluous information refers to unnecessary, excessive, or redundant details that do not add
meaning or value to a message, text, or conversation.

   ❖ Using unnecessary words: "I'm going to the store, and I will buy some milk."

(Superfluous word: "and I will")

   ❖ Providing irrelevant details: "I went to the park, which is located on Main Street, and I
     saw a dog."

(Superfluous detail: "which is located on Main Street")

   ❖ Repeating information: "I'm going to the store. The store is where I'm going."

(Superfluous sentence: "The store is where I'm going")

   ❖ Using unnecessary phrases: "To be honest with you, I don't like that movie."

(Superfluous phrase: "To be honest with you")

types of Constituents?
In linguistics, a constituent is a unit of language that consists of a group of words that function
together as a single unit. Here are the main types of constituents:

   1) Phrasal Constituent
   2) Null Constituent
   3) Clausal Constituent
   4) Lexical Constituent
   5) immediate constituents

Modal verb?
Modal verbs are auxiliary verbs that express modality, which includes notions such as possibility,
necessity, obligation, permission, ability, and prediction. Here are the main modal verbs in
English:

1. Can

2. Could

3. May

4. Might

5. Shall

6. Should

7. Will

8. Would

9. Must

To identify modal verbs, look for the following characteristics:

- They are used to express modality (possibility, necessity, obligation, etc.).

- They are auxiliary verbs, meaning they are used to help form the tense, mood, or voice of
another verb.

- They often have multiple meanings and uses.

Examples:

- "I can speak French." (ability)

- "You must try this cake." (obligation)

- "It might rain tomorrow." (possibility)

critical components of reading instruction?
the five critical components of reading instruction which include

       ❖ phonemic awareness
       ❖ decoding
       ❖ fluency
       ❖ vocabulary
       ❖ comprehension

3 semantic constraints?
Semantic constraints refer to the rules or restrictions that govern the meaning of words, phrases,
or sentences in a language. Here are three types of semantic constraints:

       1) Selectional Restrictions
       2) Presuppositional Constraints
       3) Implicational Constraints

These semantic constraints help to ensure that language is used in a way that is meaningful,
coherent, and consistent with the context.

Embedded sentence?
An embedded sentence, also known as a subordinate clause or embedded clause, is a sentence
that is nested inside another sentence. It functions as a single unit within the larger sentence.

Examples:

1. I know that she is coming. (The embedded sentence is "that she is coming.")

2. The book, which is on the table, is mine. (The embedded sentence is "which is on the table.")

Embedded sentences often begin with subordinating conjunctions, such as:

- because

- since

- after

- although

- if

- that

- which

- who

Theory of X bar?
X-bar theory is a theory of syntactic category formation. It embodies two independent claims:

One, that phrases may contain intermediate constituents projected from a head X; Two, that
this system of projected constituency may be common to more than one category (e.g., N, V, A,
P, etc.). The letter X is used to signify an arbitrary lexical category (part of speech); When
analyzing a specific utterance, specific categories are assigned. The X may become an N for
noun, a V for verb, an A for adjective, or a P for preposition. The term X-bar is derived from the
notation representing this structure. Certain structures are represented by Xˉ (an X with a bar
over it). X may be often written as X′, using the prime symbol or with superscript numerals as
exponents, e.g., X¹. In English this is still read as "X bar".

The notation XP stands for X phrase, and is at the equivalent level of X-bar-bar (X with a double
over bar), written X″ or X2 , usually read aloud as X double bar. X-bar theory was first proposed
by Noam Chomsky (1970) building on Zellig Harris's 1951 approach to categories, and further
developed by Ray Jackendoff (1977). X-bar theory was incorporated into both transformational
and nontransformational theories of syntax, including GB,etc. Recent work in the Minimalist
Program has largely abandoned Xbar schemata in favor of bare phrase structure approaches.

T-C Movement?
T-C Movement refers to the transformation of a sentence from a statement to a question, or vice
versa, by changing the position of the auxiliary verb (T) and the subject (C).

To form a question using T-C Movement, you would typically:

1. Start with a statement: "He is going to the store."

Q.What do you think are the challenges or limitations of teaching
morphology and syntax effectively discuss?
SOLUTION:
Effectively imparting the intricacies of morphology and syntax poses a formidable
challenge, given the inherent complexity of these linguistic components. One
obstacle lies in the inherent difficulty of elucidating abstract concepts such as
grammatical rules and the intricacies of word formation, particularly for learners
lacking a robust foundation in language structure. Compounding this difficulty is
the vast array of languages, each characterized by its own unique set of rules and
structures, thereby complicating the creation of universally applicable teaching
methodologies.
Furthermore, the absence of engaging and interactive resources acts as a
stumbling block to efficient learning in this domain. To surmount these
challenges, educators can leverage an arsenal of teaching tools, incorporating
visual aids, real-life examples, and interactive activities to infuse the learning
experience with both dynamism and practical relevance. Establishing a supportive
and inclusive learning environment is paramount, fostering an atmosphere where
students feel empowered to pose questions and actively refine their language
skills through practice.
By proactively addressing these hurdles and adapting teaching strategies to
accommodate the diverse needs of learners, we can significantly augment the
effectiveness of imparting knowledge in the realms of morphology and syntax.

that can be difficult for students to grasp. The intricate rules and structures
governing word formation and sentence construction may seem complex and
require a high level of abstraction.
2. Lack of Intuition: Unlike some aspects of language learning that rely on
intuition and exposure, morphology and syntax often require explicit instruction.
This lack of intuitive understanding can make it challenging for students to apply
the learned rules naturally in different linguistic contexts.
3. Diverse Language Backgrounds: Students in a language class often come from
diverse linguistic backgrounds. Teaching morphology and syntax may be more
challenging when dealing with students who speak languages with vastly different
syntactic structures and morphological systems.
4. Limited Application in Everyday Communication: Some students may struggle
to see the immediate relevance of studying morphology and syntax in everyday
communication. The abstract nature of these linguistic components may lead to a
perception that they are not as applicable in real-life language use.
5. Dynamic Nature of Language: Language is dynamic and constantly evolving.
Teaching fixed rules for morphology and syntax can be challenging as language
usage can vary over time.

Question ⁉️

What do you think are the challenges or limitations of teaching morphology and syntax effectively discuss?

Solution

Teaching morphology and syntax effectively can pose several challenges due to their abstract nature and the complex relationships between linguistic components. Here are some of the key challenges and limitations:

## 1. Abstractness of Morphology and Syntax

Morphology and syntax deal with the structure and organization of words and sentences, respectively. These concepts are abstract and often difficult to grasp for learners, especially those with limited exposure to linguistic analysis. The lack of concrete representations and real-world analogies can make it challenging to visualize and understand these concepts.

## 2. Intricacy of Grammatical Rules and Relationships

Morphology and syntax are governed by a complex set of rules and relationships between words and their grammatical functions. These rules can be intricate, nuanced, and sometimes seemingly arbitrary, making it challenging for learners to memorize and apply them consistently.

## 3. Variability and Exceptions

Language is not a rigid system; it is dynamic and ever-evolving. Morphology and syntax exhibit variability and exceptions to the established rules, further complicating the learning process. Learners may struggle to reconcile these exceptions with the general patterns they are trying to grasp.

## 4. Lack of Context and Real-World Application

Teaching morphology and syntax often focuses on isolated grammatical forms and structures, which can limit learners' understanding of their actual usage and function in real-world language. Without contextualization and opportunities to apply these concepts in meaningful communication, learners may struggle to see their relevance and practical application.

## 5. Overemphasis on Formal Rules and Terminology

Focusing solely on formal rules and grammatical terminology can make morphology and syntax appear dry and intimidating, hindering learners' engagement and motivation. A more interactive and engaging approach that emphasizes patterns, connections, and real-world usage can make these concepts more accessible and relatable.

## 6. Individual Learning Styles and Abilities

Learners have different learning styles, preferences, and levels of linguistic aptitude. Teaching morphology and syntax effectively requires adapting to these individual differences, providing varied instructional methods, and offering personalized support to ensure that all learners can progress at their own pace and reach their full potential.

## 7. Limited Resources and Teacher Training

Effective teaching of morphology and syntax often requires access to well-designed instructional materials, supplementary resources, and ongoing teacher training. Limited availability of these resources and opportunities for professional development can hinder teachers' ability to effectively implement engaging and effective teaching strategies.

## 8. Cultural and Linguistic Diversity

In multilingual classrooms, teachers face the additional challenge of accommodating learners with diverse linguistic backgrounds and cultural contexts. Tailoring instruction to address these differences and ensuring that all learners feel included and supported can be a significant challenge.

## 9. Assessment and Evaluation

Assessing learners' understanding of morphology and syntax can be challenging due to the abstract nature of these concepts and the variability of language usage. Developing effective assessment tools that accurately gauge learners' comprehension and application of these concepts is crucial for providing meaningful feedback and guiding further instruction.

Overcoming these challenges requires a combination of pedagogical expertise, creativity, and a commitment to providing individualized support. By addressing the abstractness and complexity of morphology and syntax, incorporating real-world applications, and adapting to diverse learning styles, teachers can foster a deeper understanding and appreciation of these fundamental aspects of language.

ENG509_Glossary

1. A-head :An A-head is the kind of head (like T) which allows as its specifier an
   argument expression but not an adjunct expression. An A-bar head is the kind of
   head (like C) which allows as its specifier either an argument or an adjunct
   expression.
2. A-movement :Movement from one A-position to another (typically, from a
   subject or complement position into another subject position).
3. Acronym :A word derived by taking the initial letter of all or most words in a
   string and pronouncing them together,
4. Allomorph :a variant form of a morpheme, that is, when a unit of meaning varies
   in sound without changing the meaning.
5. Constituent structure :The constituent structure (or phrase structure, or
   syntactic structure) of an expression is (a representation of) the set of constituents
   which the expression contains. Syntactic structure is usually represented in terms
   of a labelled bracketing or a tree diagram.
6. Derivation :the formation of a new word from another word or stem. It typically
   occurs by the addition of an affix.
7. Determiner :A word like the/this/that which is typically used to modify a noun,
   but which has no descriptive content of its own.
8. Ditransitive :A ditransitive structure is a double-object structure like ‘She gave
   me them’, where the transitive verb gave has two objects (me and them).
9. Headedness Principle :An expression is headed if it has a head. The Headedness
   Principle specifies that every constituent must be headed (i.e. must have a head).
   So, for example, an expression like ‘fond of fast food’ is headed by the adjective
   fond and so is an adjectival phrase.

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG509_Glossary

10. Inflection :a change in or addition to the form of a word that shows a change
   in the way it is used in sentences
11. Lexeme :a basic lexical unit of a language consisting of one word or several
   words, the elements of which do not separately convey the meaning of the whole.
12. Lexicon :a lexicon is a language's inventory of lexemes
13. Morpheme :a meaningful morphological unit of a language that cannot be
   further divided (e.g. in, come, -ing, forming incoming
14. Morphological derivation :the process of forming a new word from an
   existing word, often by adding a prefix or suffix
15. Morphology :the study of words, how they are formed, and their relationship
   to other words in the same language
16. Morphosyntax :An area of linguistics that deals with the relationship and
   interactions between morphology (the structure of words) and syntax (the
   structure of larger utterances, such as phrases and sentences).
17. Phonology :the study of how sounds are organized and used in natural
   languages
18. Syntax :the arrangement of words and phrases to create well-formed
   sentences in a language
19. Tense :The inflectional category that indicates the time an event or action took
   place relative to the time of utterance.
20. Transitive verb: A verb that takes a direct object, e.g., writes.
21. Wh-movement: Transformation that moves a question word or phrase from
   a theoretically posited lower position in a sentence to a higher one in question
   formation.

By ASFAND YARR

                            ENG509_Glossary

22. Zero-derivation: A word-formation process that changes the lexical category
   of a word without changing its phonological shape. Also called conversion.

eng509-important-terms-pdf:
ENG509
➡️ Morphemes
Morphemes are minimal units of meaning within words.

➡️ What is a Word?
A word is a unit of language conveying meaning.

➡️ Types of Words
-   Free morphemes (standalone words)
-   Bound morphemes (prefixes, suffixes)
-   Inflected words (changed form)
-   Derived words (new meaning)

➡️ Empirical Tests for Wordhood
Tests determine word status:
-   Phonological criteria
-   Syntactic criteria
-   Semantic criteria

➡️ Inflection vs. Derivation
-   Inflection: modifies word form (tense, number)
-   Derivation: creates new word (prefixes, suffixes)

➡️ Two Approaches to Morphology
-   Item-and-Arrangement: focuses on morpheme combination
-   Item-and-Process: emphasizes word formation processes

➡️ Primary and Secondary Affixes
-   Primary affixes: directly attach to roots
-   Secondary affixes: attach to derived words

➡️ Linguistic Exaptation, Levelling, and Analogy
-   Exaptation: reuses existing structures
-   Levelling: simplifies irregularities
-   Analogy: creates new forms based on patterns

➡️ The Saussurean Sign
The Saussurean sign represents the relationship between signifier and signified.

➡️ Motivation and Compositionality
-   Motivation: iconic or arbitrary
-   Compositionality: meaning derived from parts
Zero Derivation

Q. give 2 characteristic features of inflection and derivation
Inflection involves the formation of grammatical forms – past, present, future; singular, plural; masculine, feminine, neuter; and so on – of a single lexeme. The use of these grammatical forms is generally dictated by sentence structure. Thus is, are, and being are examples of inflected forms of the lexeme be, Regular verb lexemes in English have a lexical stem, which is the bare form with no affixes (e.g., select) and three more inflected forms, one each with the suffixes -s, -ed, and -ing .
Derivation involves the creation of one lexeme from another, Compounding is a special type of derivation, since it involves the creation of one lexeme from two or more other lexemes.
1. Bookshop,
2. greenhouse
Derivation generally results in a change in lexical meaning or the lexical category of a particular word, while inflection does not

Q. Universal Grammer.
Universal Grammar is the theory developed by Noam Chomsky that states that all languages are identical at some level of analysis. Tremendous influence on the field of linguistics, and most linguists agree with Chomsky that language has an innate component.  A key phrase in the definition of Universal Grammar that we have provided is “at some level of analysis.”  What is the level of analysis at which languages are identical? Q. Headed and headless compounds and example.5 marks
Cultural and technical change produces more novel artefacts than novel activities or novel properties.  These changes therefore generate new vocabulary needs that are more readily answered by new nouns than by new verbs or adjectives.
Examples can be found with each of the other main word classes supplying the left-hand element:
    1.  verb–noun (VN): swearword, drophammer, playtime
    2. noun–noun (NN): hairnet, mosquito net, butterfly net, hair restorer
    3. adjective–noun (AN): blackboard, greenstone, faintheart
    4. preposition–noun (PN): in-group, outpost, overcoat
All of these have the main stress on the left – a characteristic important for distinguishing compound nouns from noun phrases.
The difference in precision with which we can interpret hair restorer on the one hand and hairnet etc. on the other hinges on the fact that restorer in hair restorer is derived from a verb (restore).  Verbs, unlike most nouns and adjectives, impose expectations and requirements on the noun phrases that accompany them in the sentence.
For example, an X-restorer, whatever X is, something or someone that restores X.

    1. Sign-writer,
    2. slum clearance,
    3. crime prevention,
    4. wish-fulfillment.

Q. Example of root compounding

Q. why children over extend the words tree/plants

Overextend tree by using it to refer to potted plants, trees, and even balsam fir wreaths. Such
under- and overextensions are generally short-lived, which indicates that children revise lexical
entries as they are exposed to more and more tokens of a word.

words

Q. defines the term exocentricity in the content of morphology.

Exocentric construction cannot be substituted for any of its element and thus has no head. For
Example: Is not an expansion of with a or paper. Not an expansion of any of its parts. An
exocentric construction cannot be substituted for any of its element and thus has no head.

Q. Explain linguistic junk

Rudes (1980) and Lass (1990) have both raised the question of what to do with “linguistic
leftovers” or “linguistic junk” (Lass’s term). In both cases, it has to do with morphemes that lose
their semantic content or morphosyntactic function as a result of language change and are left as
content less, functionless strings of phonemes floating around in the system. They show that
languages are in general intolerant of useless elements, and speakers reanalyze them as having a
new role. Lass call this process lingic exaptation, extending a term of evolutionary biology to the
study of lang change.

Q. Define Polosemey (3)

 The most fundamental aspect of a word’s meaning is that it refers to some entity or relation
(realor imaginary) in the world. We can refer to this entity or relation as the word’s semantic
type. Formal approaches to grammar have provided us with terminology that allows us to make

                              ENG509 (MIDS) Fall2019

evenmore fine-tuned distinctions between words. The word reptile refers to all individuals in
theworld that are reptiles. Verbs like respect or love refer to relationships between individuals. q.
Three types of polysemy There are many types of polysemy.

   (1) mass/count distinction a. I love watermelon. (mass) b. I sold three watermelons. (count)
   (2) Figure–ground reversal a. Hugh broke the window. b. The kids climbed through the
       window.

Q. Prepositional phrases. Two examples.
Two examples:
   1. The cupcake with sprinkles is yours.
   2. We climbed up the hill.
   3. The rabbits hopped through the garden.
In these examples, with sprinkles, up the hill and through the garden are prepositional phrases.
Q. Transitive verbs. Two examples.
Two examples:
   1. She left (transitive verb) the keys (direct object) on the table.
   2. My father took (transitive verb) me (direct object) to the movies for my birthday.
   Q. Verb phrases. Two examples.
Two examples:
   1. As the cat watched, the two puppies fought over a bone.
   2. Walking on the ice, she slipped and fell.
   3. Finally, we can afford to buy a new house.
In these examples, as the cat watched, walking on the ice and to buy a new house are verb phrases.

Q. Types of phrases.
   1. Noun Phrase: A group of words in a sentence that acts like a noun is called a “Noun Phrase”.
   2. Verb Phrase: A group of words consisting of one main verb and one or more helping verbs is called a
      “Verb Phrase”.
   3. Adjective Phrase: A group of words that describes a noun in a sentence is known as an “Adjective
      Phrase”.
   4. Prepositional Phrase: A group of words consisting of a preposition, followed by a noun, verb, a pronoun
      or a noun phrase is called a “Prepositional Phrase”.
   5. Adverb Phrase: A group of words that describes a verb, adjective or other adverb in a sentence.
Q. Four types of determiner.
Types of Determiners:
1. Articles:
There are three articles in English language: a, an, the. The articles “a” and “an” are used when we need to clarify
the noun as indefinite and singular. The article “a” comes before nouns beginning with a constant sound, while the
article “an” comes before nouns beginning with a vowel sound. The article “the” is used when we need to clarify
the noun as definite and unique.
Example of Articles:
      We saw the car again today.
      I am going to read a newspaper.
      She has an umbrella.
2. Demonstratives:
The category of words which is used to clarify the distance of something or some person from the speaker is called
demonstratives.
Use of Demonstratives in a Sentence:
Demonstratives can function as adjectives and pronouns in a sentence.
These include: That, These, This, Those.
“That” is used when a singular noun is not very close to the speaker. “This” is used when a singular noun is
precisely in front and close to the speaker. “Those” is used when plural nouns are not very close to the speaker.
“These” is used when plural nouns are precisely in front and close to the speaker.
Examples of Demonstratives:
      That is the place I want to go to.
      These books are fun to read.

3. Possessives:
The words that come to modify a noun to indicate possession towards some person or something are called
possessives.
These include: your, our, my, his, hers, its, their etc
Examples of Possessives:

             (Eng509) Morphology and Syntax                  Solved Fall18 Past Papers by 2nd Batch

          I am doing my assignment.
          This dress is hers.
    4. Quantifiers
    The category of indefinite determiners which is used to indicate the quantity of the noun without stating the precise
    number is called the Quantifiers.
    These include: many, much, plenty, enough, several, some, few, little etc.
    Examples of quantifiers:
          I took out some vegetables from the fridge.
          She has several friends at school who work part-time.
          He does not have many friends.

    Do-support (or do-insertion), in English grammar, is the use of the auxiliary verb do, including it's inflected forms

    inversion is required. Do-support is not used when there is already an auxiliary or copular verb present or with

    Do-support appears to accommodate a number of varying grammatical constructions:
          Question formation,
          The appearance of the negation not, and

13.SVO is the basic word order of ------------------. (English)
14.The passive involves promotion of an object phrase to a new position in the sentence, known
   as the subject position. (True)
15.At what age, children can acquire native like syntactic competence? (9 or 10)
16.Run’ is a two-morpheme word. (False)
17.Chomsky claims human beings are biologically endowed with an innate language faculty.
   (True)
18.English is a non-null-subject language. (True)
19.At what age, children generally produce their first recognizable word (e.g. Mama or Dada)?
   (12)
20.Each word consists of one or two morphemes. (True)
21.John laughed. In this sentence John is a ___phrase. (Noun)
22.‘IC’ analysis stands for Immediate Constituent. (True)
23.The clause is regarded as the largest or highest unit on the hierarchical scale of constituents.
   (False)
24.The syntactic analysis of the sentence does not usually go below the level of the word. (True)
25.Cleft sentence is considered a sentence in which some part is moved from its normal position
   into a different place to give it more emphasis. (True)
26.Pseudo-cleft sentence is a kind of cleft sentence in which the subordinated clause is a relative
   clause headed by an interrogative pro-form. (True)

                             Quiz from Assessments (Mid-Term)

1. The word ‘fish’ takes no morpheme when becomes plural. (True)
2. Phonology is the branch of linguistics that deals with words, their internal structure, and how
   they are formed. (False)
3. Stem is the base unit to which another morphological piece is attached. (True)
4. The word ‘morphology’ belongs to ------------- language. (Greek)
5. The branch of linguistics that allows creating new and unique words is called ------------.
   (Morphology)
6. ‘Analysis’ and ‘-------------’ are the two basic approaches to morphological analysis.
   (synthesis)
7. Item-and-arrangement and item-and-process are the two approaches to morphology. (True)
8. Inflection is the process of forming different grammatical forms of a single lexeme? (True)
9. Derivation is the process of creating one lexeme from another. (True)
10.Noun is the word which can be the subject of a sentence. (True)
11.Which of the following is the content word? (Bargain)
12.The word lexicon is from ------------ lexikós means ‘pertaining to words’. (Greek)
13.When two or more instances of a given morpheme occur with different shapes, we call them
   allomorphs. (True)
14.Which of the following branches of linguistics deals with the interaction of morphology and
   prosodic structure? (Prosodic Morphology)
15.__________ deals with restrictions in a language on the permissible combinations of
   phonemes. (Phonotactics)
16._______________ describes the interactions taking place between morphology and
   phonology. (Morphophonology)
17.The phenomenon whereby a language becomes intolerant of ------------- elements and speakers
   reanalyze them as having a new role is called linguistic exaptation. (useless)
18.Identify the secret language from the given options. (Pig Latin)
19.The idea that language is a system of signs was proposed by --------------. (Ferdinand de
   Saussure)
20.Identify the example of clipping from the following options. (Typo)
21.Which of the following is the process of creating a word by removing what appears to be an
   affix? (Backformation)
22.Clipping is the process of creating a new word by truncation of an existing one. (True)
23.Zero-derivation changes the lexical category of a word without changing its ------------ shape.
   (phonological)
24.The noun -------------takes an irregular suffix to form its plural. (child)
25.Identify the determiner from the given options. (This)
26.The noun -------------takes a zero suffix to form its plural. (sheep)
27.Performs, performed and perform all are the inflected forms of the lexeme perform. (True)

28.In English, a verb lexeme has at most five distinct forms (True)
29.English adjectives have mostly three forms. (True)
30.Identify the regular suffix to form plural of nouns. (-s)
31.Identify the noun from the following which is formed by changing the vowel of its verb. (Song)
32.Identify the noun from the following which is formed by changing the final consonant of its
   verb. (Proof)
33.Identify the noun from the following which is formed by changing the vowel of its verb. (seat)
34.‘Performance’ and ------------- are the two forms of a lexeme ‘Performance’. (Performances)
35.Identify the verb which is formed by replacing the final voiceless consonant of its noun with a
   voiced one. (Bathe)
36.Identify the noun from the following which is formed by changing the vowel of its verb. (Song)
37.Identify the compound verb type that describes ‘blackboard’. (Adjective-noun (AN))
38.Phrasal words have the internal structure of phrases but function syntactically as words. (True)
39.Noun-verb (NV) is the compound verb type that describes ‘stir-fry’. (False)
40.Playtime is an example of the left-headed compound. (True)
41.Verb-noun (VN) is the compound verb type that describes ‘playtime’. (True)
42.Identify the headless compound from the given options. (Faint-heart)
43.In the word ‘undividable’, the prefix un- conveys the meaning of --------------. (not)
44.In a/an ------------- compound word, none of its units represents the properties that the word
   exhibits. (exocentric)
45.A-Morphous Morphology claims that words do not have an internal structure. (True)
46.Third kind of paradox takes into account phonological factors. (True)
47.Parasynthesis is the situation where two different affixes - a prefix and a suffix - seem to be
   added simultaneously to the same base. (True)
48.Identify the category of the word ‘undesirable’ from the given options. (Adjective)
49.Which of the following options conveys the meaning of the prefix re- in the word ‘reassemble’?
   (Again)
50.Identify the option which is NOT an agent. (Screwdriver)
51.Which of the following is the capacity of a word to have multiple meanings? (Polysemy)

What is Morphology?
Morphology is the study of the internal structure of words and how they are
formed from smaller units like roots, prefixes, and suffixes.
Example: "unhappiness" can be broken down into its morphological
components: "un-" (prefix) + "happi-" (root) + "-ness" (suffix).
   Words and Lexemes: A word is a unit of language with a specific meaning,
   while a lexeme is the base form of a word without inflections.
   Morphology and Phonology
Morphology deals with the structure of words, while phonology focuses on the
sound system of language.
Example: "bat" and "hat" differ phonologically (sound), but are similar
morphologically (structure).
   Derivation and the Lexicon
Derivation involves adding affixes to roots to form new words, which are stored
in the mental lexicon.
Example: "happy" (root) + "-ness" (suffix) = "happiness" (derived word).
   Words & Forms: Inflections
Inflections are morphological changes that indicate grammatical function, like
tense or number.
Example: "walk" (base form) vs. "walked" (inflected form).
   Words & Its Relatives: Derivation

Derivation creates new words by adding affixes, like -ed or -ness, to roots.
Example: "create" (root) + "-ion" (suffix) = "creation" (derived word).
   Morphological Structures
Morphological structures include roots, prefixes, and suffixes that combine to
form words.
Example: "un-" (prefix) + "break-" (root) + "-able" (suffix) = "unbreakable".
   Derivation and Semantics
Derivation can change the meaning of a word, like adding -ful to create an
adjective.
Example: "hope" (root) + "-ful" (suffix) = "hopeful" (derived adjective).
   Inflections
Inflections are morphological changes that indicate grammatical function, like
tense or number.
Example: "go" (base form) vs. "went" (inflected form).
   Lexical Source of English Word Formation
English words can come from various sources, including Latin, Greek, and
Germanic roots.
Example: "captain" comes from Latin "capitaneus".
   Morphological Productivity and the Mental Lexicon
The mental lexicon stores words and their morphological structures, allowing for
productive word formation.
Example: "un-" (prefix) + "happi-" (root) + "-ness" (suffix) = "unhappiness"
(productively formed word).
   Morphology and Syntax
Morphology studies word structure, while syntax examines how words combine
to form sentences.

Example: "The dog chased the cat." (syntax) vs. "dog" (morphology).
   Morphology and Psycholinguistics
Morphology is related to psycholinguistics, as it involves the mental
representation and processing of words.
Example: How we process and store morphological information in our mental
lexicon.
   Morphology and Language Change
Morphological structures can change over time, influencing language evolution.
Example: Old English "hwaet" (root) + "-er" (suffix) = "whater" (derived word),
which became Modern English "water".
   Traditional Grammar: Categories & Functions
Traditional grammar categorizes words into parts of speech based on their
functions. The main categories are:
    Nouns (N): words that refer to people, places, things, or ideas (e.g., "dog",
     "city", "happiness")
    Verbs (V): words that express actions, events, or states (e.g., "run", "eat",
     "be")
    Adjectives (Adj): words that modify nouns or pronouns (e.g., "happy",
     "big", "blue")
    Adverbs (Adv): words that modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs
     (e.g., "quickly", "very", "well")
    Pronouns (Pron): words that replace nouns in a sentence (e.g., "he",
     "she", "it")
    Prepositions (Prep): words that show relationships between words in a
     sentence (e.g., "in", "on", "under")
    Conjunctions (Conj): words that connect words, phrases, or clauses (e.g.,
     "and", "but", "or")
    Interjections (Int): words that express emotion or feeling (e.g., "oh",
     "ouch", "wow")
   What is Syntax?

Syntax is the study of how words are combined to form phrases, clauses, and
sentences. It examines the rules and patterns that govern the structure of
language.
Example: "The dog chased the cat."
    "The dog" is a noun phrase (NP) functioning as the subject.
    "chased" is a verb (V) functioning as the predicate.
    "the cat" is a noun phrase (NP) functioning as the object.
   Universal Grammar
Universal Grammar (UG) is a theoretical framework that proposes all humans
are born with an innate capacity for language, including a set of universal
principles and constraints that shape language acquisition and use.
Example: All languages have a subject-verb-object word order, despite
differences in language-specific grammar rules.
   Sentence Presenting Constituency Tests
Constituency tests are used to identify the constituent structure of a sentence,
which reveals how words group together to form phrases and clauses.
Example: "The man in the corner is reading a book."
 "The man in the corner" is a noun phrase (NP) functioning as the subject.
 "is reading" is a verb phrase (VP) functioning as the predicate.
 "a book" is a noun phrase (NP) functioning as the object.
  Constituents: Words Order
Words can be ordered in different ways to form phrases and sentences.
Example: "The dog bit the man." vs. "The man was bitten by the dog."
Both sentences have the same words, but the word order changes the sentence
structure and meaning.
   Constituents: Phrases
Phrases are groups of words that function together as a unit.

Example: "The big red car" is a noun phrase (NP) consisting of an article ("The"),
an adjective ("big"), another adjective ("red"), and a noun ("car").
   Content words and Function words
Content words carry meaning, while function words indicate grammatical
relationships.
Example: "The dog ran quickly."
    "dog" is a content word (noun) carrying meaning.
    "The" is a function word (article) indicating the noun's grammatical
     function.
    "ran" is a content word (verb) carrying meaning.
    "quickly" is a function word (adverb) modifying the verb.

   What is Syntax?

Syntax is the study of how words are combined to form phrases, clauses, and
sentences. It examines the rules and patterns that govern the structure of
language.
Example: "The dog chased the cat."
    "The dog" is a noun phrase (NP) functioning as the subject.
    "chased" is a verb (V) functioning as the predicate.
    "the cat" is a noun phrase (NP) functioning as the object.
   Universal Grammar
Universal Grammar (UG) is a theoretical framework that proposes all humans
are born with an innate capacity for language, including a set of universal
principles and constraints that shape language acquisition and use.
Example: All languages have a subject-verb-object word order, despite
differences in language-specific grammar rules.
   Sentence Presenting Constituency Tests
Constituency tests are used to identify the constituent structure of a sentence,
which reveals how words group together to form phrases and clauses.
Example: "The man in the corner is reading a book."
 "The man in the corner" is a noun phrase (NP) functioning as the subject.
 "is reading" is a verb phrase (VP) functioning as the predicate.
 "a book" is a noun phrase (NP) functioning as the object.
  Constituents: Words Order
Words can be ordered in different ways to form phrases and sentences.
Example: "The dog bit the man." vs. "The man was bitten by the dog."
Both sentences have the same words, but the word order changes the sentence
structure and meaning.
   Constituents: Phrases
Phrases are groups of words that function together as a unit.

Example: "The big red car" is a noun phrase (NP) consisting of an article ("The"),
an adjective ("big"), another adjective ("red"), and a noun ("car").
   Content words and Function words
Content words carry meaning, while function words indicate grammatical
relationships.
Example: "The dog ran quickly."
    "dog" is a content word (noun) carrying meaning.
    "The" is a function word (article) indicating the noun's grammatical
     function.
    "ran" is a content word (verb) carrying meaning.
    "quickly" is a function word (adverb) modifying the verb.

How is the word class to which a lexeme belongs determined?

      Morphology is the part of linguistics that studies grammatical properties of words and

        In English grammar and morphology, a morpheme is a meaningful linguistic unit
consisting of a word such as dog, or a word element, such as the -s at the end of dogs, that can't
be divided into smaller meaningful parts.
Morphemes are the smallest units of meaningin a language. They are commonly classified as
either free morphemes, which can occur as separate words or bound morphemes, which can't
stand alone as words.

following sentence is a distinct morpheme: "I need to go now, but you can stay." Put another
way, none of the nine words in that sentence can be divided into smaller parts that are also
meaningful.

Q. Define the term right headed compound

All these compounds have a verb as the rightmost element, and also that, with most of them, the
activity denoted by the compound as whole is a variety of the activity denoted by that rightmost
element. Let us call these compounds right-headed, the rightmost element being the head. Most
English compounds are right-headed, but not all. As with verbs, it is the type with the preposition
over as its first element that seems most productive, in that new adjectives of this type, with the
meaning ‘too X’, are readily acceptable: for example, overindignant, oversmooth.

Example:

    1. noun–adjective (NA): sky-high, coal-black, oil-rich
    2. adjective–adjective (AA): grey-green, squeaky-clean, red-hot
    3. preposition–adjective (PA): under full, overactive

Q. Explain the concept of phonotactic constraint with one example.

Phonotactics is a branch of phonology that deals with restrictions in a language on the
permissible combinations of phonemes. Phonotactic constraints

twelfths /twɛlfθs/

/s/ + /t/ + /j/ (not in most accents of American English)

/s/ + /p/ + /j ɹ l/

/s/ + /k/ + /j ɹ l w/

At their most basic, phonotactic constraints determine the minimum length of content words in
particular languages. For example, in Mohawk, each content word contains at least two syllables
(Michelson 1988, cited by Hayes 1995: 47). Other languages require that content words consist
of at least a heavy syllable. In Mayan languages, roots are predominantly of the shape CVC and
in Bantu they are generally CVCV. In Semitic languages, roots consist of three consonants:
CCC.

Q. Explain the concept of bracketing paradox briefly.

There are three kinds of bracketing paradox

1.One kind of bracketing paradox is the situation in which the formal properties of one of the
units requires it to combine with a particular base, but the meaning of the word suggests that it
combines with a unit smaller than the base.Take the word international. The formal properties of
the word require the prefix inter- to combine with the adjective national, as the word *internation
does not exist in English

2. Another kind of paradox comes when a unit combines with a word but semantically modifies
not only the word, but a bigger structure in which the word is included. Consider the expression
Vulgar Latinist. This does not refer to Latinist who happens to be Vulgar, but to someone who
studies Vulgar Latin

3. Last kind of paradox take into account phonological factors. In the case unhappy, there is a
paradox in the sense that the meaning of the adjective (more unhappy) require the suffix –er to
combine with the trisyllabic adjective unhappy. It is known that generally trisyllabic adjective
take the adverb more in the comparative. Avoiding this phonological infraction implies
proposing that –er combines with happy and then un- is combines with happier. This gives the
wrong semantics as it mean; not more happy’ which the speaker does not interpret. There is no
analysis for bracketing in the general case which cover the three paradoxes

Q. Explain the direct and indirect route with reference to morphological processing of a
compound word.

The insight that complex words are often stored as such in the lexicon raises the question of how
they are processed. There are two ways in which a complex word can be processed, the direct
route, and the indirect route. When perception of complex words is involved, the direct route
means that we do not first parse the complex word, but go directly to its representation in the
lexicon, in order to access its meaning. The indirect route means that a complex word is parsed
into constituent morphemes, and that its meaning is computed after we have gained access to its
constituent morphemes and their meanings. There are data that might be interpreted as showing
that language users try to parse wods into morphological subconstituents

There are many types of polysemy.

(1)mass/count distinction

a. I love watermelon. (mass)       b. I sold three watermelons. (count)

(2) Figure–ground reversal

a. Hugh broke the window.      b. The kids climbed through the window.

(3) Container– contained alternation

a. A hot glass put under cold water will shatter.   b. Franny downed the glass in two seconds

Q. active vocabulary and Passive vocabulary

The number of words that you understand. The active vocabulary, the set of words one uses in
language production is much smaller. A dictionary is conservative by nature, and hence it will
contain words from the past that nobody uses any more. Mental lexicon will always be ahead of
the dictionary, and contains a substantial number of words that are not listed in dictionaries. New
words (neologisms) are coined continuously, and dictionaries always lag behind.

Q. Differentiate betwen competence n performance

The lexeme performance denotes the same activity, surely. Does that mean that perform and
performance belong to the same word class? Perform has four forms: perform, perform,
performing and performed. Performance has two: performance and performances

Competence is Chomsky’s (1965) term for the knowledge that speakers and hearers have of their
language. Some people would say that productivity is not part of linguistic competence either,
because, in order for something to be considered part of competence, it must be structural and
‘all or none’. Productivity is a probabilistic notion, and some linguists believe that if something
is probabilistic, it is not structural and hence is not part of the grammar. Under this view,
productivity would have to be treated as a phenomenon that is related to a speaker’s competence,
but not part of it.
